raw_answer_text:
A1: The unicast routing table (RIB), which is also used to derive the router's understanding of reverse paths.
A2: The packet's source address is used as the lookup key.
A3: It also tells the router the next-hop (upstream) neighbor and the metric/preference associated with that path, along with the expected incoming interface.
A4: It compares that interface against the interface on which the multicast packet actually arrived.
A5: The router first looks up the route back toward the source, then compares it to the arrival interface.
A6: The packet passes if the expected interface (from the source lookup) matches the interface on which it arrived; when it passes, the router forwards it out the appropriate outgoing interface(s) per the multicast forwarding state.
A7: The packet fails if the arrival interface does not match the expected interface toward the source; when it fails, the router drops the packet.
A8: It's called "reverse" because instead of checking the route toward the destination (as normal unicast forwarding does), it checks the route back toward the source of the traffic, verifying the packet arrived from the direction it should have come from.
